'''Carl Benjamin Boyer''' (November 3, 1906 – April 26, 1976) was an American historian of [[mathematics]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |date=April 27, 1976 |title=Carl Boyer dies, a mathematician |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1976/04/27/archives/carl-boyer-dies-a-mathematician-brooklyn-professor-wrote-histories.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221116023444/https://www.nytimes.com/1976/04/27/archives/carl-boyer-dies-a-mathematician-brooklyn-professor-wrote-histories.html |archive-date=November 16, 2022 |access-date=March 20, 2026 |work=The New York Times |pages=37}}</ref> dubbed the "[[Edward Gibbon|Gibbon]] of [[History of mathematics|math history]]" by novelist [[David Foster Wallace]].<ref>{{cite web| author=Wallace, David Foster|author-link=David Foster Wallace|title=An excerpt from ''Everything and More''|url=http://www.conjunctions.com/webcon/wallace.htm|access-date=2007-08-28| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120219093659/https://www.conjunctions.com/webcon/wallace.htm| archive-date= 2012-02-19| url-status= dead}}</ref> He was one of few historians of mathematics of his time to "keep open links with contemporary history of science."<ref>{{Cite book |last=Remmert |first=Volker R. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iKCwDQAAQBAJ&q=open+links&pg=PA161 |title=Historiography of Mathematics in the 19th and 20th Centuries |last2=Schneider |first2=Martina R. |last3=Sørensen |first3=Henrik Kragh |date=2016-12-08 |publisher=Birkhäuser |isbn=978-3-319-39649-1 |language=en}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=161}}

==Early life and education==
Boyer was born in [[Hellertown, Pennsylvania]], on November 3, 1906, and graduated as [[valedictorian]] of his [[high school]] class. He received a bachelor's degree from [[Columbia College of Columbia University|Columbia College]] in 1928 and started working as a tutor at [[Brooklyn College]] in the same year. From [[Columbia University]], he earned his master's degree in 1929 and his doctorate in history in 1939.<ref name=":0" /> He was a full professor of mathematics at Brooklyn College from 1952 until his death.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Writing the History of Mathematics: Its Historical Development |publisher=Birkhäuser |year=2002 |isbn=978-3-764-36167-9 |editor-last=Dauben |editor-first=Joseph W. |editor-link=Joseph Dauben |editor-last2=Scriba |editor-first2=Christoph J.|editor2-link=Christoph Scriba}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=380-1}}

==Career==
Along with [[Carolyn Eisele]] of CUNY's [[Hunter College]]; [[C. Doris Hellman]] of the [[Pratt Institute]], and later [[City University of New York]]'s [[Queens College]]; and [[Lynn Thorndike]] of Columbia University, Boyer was instrumental in the 1953 founding of the Metropolitan New York Section of the [[History of Science Society]].<ref>Gleason, Mary Louise (1999) [https://www.jstor.org/stable/238014 "The Metropolitan New York Section of the History of Science Society"], ''Isis'', Vol. 90, Supplement: ''Catching up with the Vision: Essays on the Occasion of the 75th Anniversary of the Founding of the History of Science Society'', pp. S200-S218. University of Chicago Press on behalf of The History of Science Society</ref>

In 1954, Boyer was the recipient of a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] to further his work in the history of science, in particular, the history of the study of rainbows.<ref>Staff (May 3, 1954) [https://timesmachine.nytimes.com/timesmachine/1954/05/03/92826911.pdf "Guggenheim Fund Grants $1,000,000"] ''[[The New York Times]]''</ref>

Boyer wrote the books ''The History of the Calculus and Its Conceptual Development'' (1959),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boyer |first=Carl B. |title=The History of the Calculus and Its Conceptual Development |publisher=Dover |year=2012 |isbn=978-0-486-60509-8 |location=New York |orig-year=1959}}</ref> which was originally published as ''The Concepts of the Calculus'' (1939).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boyer |first=Carl B. |title=The Concepts of the Calculus |publisher=Hafner Pub. Co. |year=1949 |location=New York |oclc=1425849052}}</ref> [[Richard Courant]] wrote the foreword to the second edition (1949).<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Kline |first=Morris |author-link=Morris Kline |date=November 1976 |title=Carl B. Boyer—in memoriam |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/031508607690063X |journal=Historia Mathematica |volume=3 |issue=4 |pages=387–394}}</ref> This was his first book. In it, Boyer examined the [[history of calculus]] from the time of the [[Ancient Greek mathematics|ancient Greeks]] to the nineteenth century, when calculus was put in a [[Rigour#Mathematics|rigorous]] foundation thanks to the contributions of [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy]], [[Karl Weierstrass]], and others.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Byrne |first=W. E. |date=April 1940 |title=Reviewed Work: ''The Concepts of the Calculus'' by Carl B. Boyer |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3028925 |journal=[[National Mathematics Magazine]] |volume=14 |issue=7 |pages=427 |doi=10.2307/3028925|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Boyer then accomplished a similar feat with ''History of [[Analytic geometry|Analytic Geometry]]'' (1956),<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boyer |first=Carl B. |title=History of Analytic Geometry |publisher=Scripta Mathematica |year=1956 |location=New York |oclc=260863}}</ref> presenting the developments from antiquity in [[Mesopotamia]] and [[Ancient Egyptian mathematics|Egypt]], to the independent creation of the subject proper by [[Pierre de Fermat]] and [[René Descartes]], and to the third quarter of the nineteenth century with the contributions of [[August Ferdinand Möbius]], [[Julius Plücker]], and [[Arthur Cayley]].<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rosenthal |first=Arthur |author-link=Arthur Rosenthal |date=April 1957 |title=''History of Analytic Geometry''. Carl B. Boyer. Scripta Mathematica, Yeshiva University, New York, 1956. 291 pp. Illus. $6. |journal=Science |publisher=American Association for the Advancement of Science |volume=125 |issue=3252 |pages=823–4 |doi=10.1126/science.125.3252.823}}</ref> Boyer gave 76 key [[primary source]]s in roughly chronological order at the end of the book.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eves |first=Howard |date=September 1957 |title=Book Review: ''History of Analytic Geometry'' by C. B. Boyer |journal=[[The American Mathematical Monthly]] |doi=10.2307/2308483}}</ref> He followed this with ''The Rainbow: From Myth to Mathematics'' (1959).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boyer |first=Carl B. |title=The Rainbow from Myth to Mathematics |publisher=T. Yoseloff |year=1959 |location=New York |oclc=538512}}</ref>

Boyer published ''A History of Mathematics'' in 1968.<ref name=":1" /> This book broke new grounds by discussing mathematics developed during the early twentieth century.<ref name=":3" /> After he died in 1976, [[Uta Merzbach]], a historian of mathematics at the [[Smithsonian Institution]], took responsibility for revising and updating the text. The second edition appeared in 1991, with a foreword by [[Isaac Asimov]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Acker |first=Kathleen |date=July 2007 |title=Review: ''A History of Mathematics'' |url=https://old.maa.org/press/periodicals/convergence/history-of-mathematics |journal=Convergence |publisher=Mathematical Association of America}}</ref> She released the third edition in 2011.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Boyer |first=Carl B. |title=A History of Mathematics |last2=Merzbach |first2=Uta |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-470-52548-7 |edition=3rd |location=New York}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Graham |first=Jason M. |date=April 17, 2017 |title=''A History of Mathematics'' |url=https://old.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/a-history-of-mathematics-0 |journal=MAA Reviews |publisher=Mathematical Association of America}}</ref> Since its first edition, it has become a standard text on the subject.<ref name=":3" /> Reviewers praised this book for its broad and accessible coverage of interesting developments from antiquity to the modern era.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> However, the third edition contains no exercises at the end of each chapter.<ref name=":2" /> Jason Graham noted that readers interested in more technical details could supplement the book with ''A History of Mathematics'' (2009) by [[Victor J. Katz|Victor Katz]] or ''The Fontana History of the Mathematical Sciences'' (1997) by [[Ivor Grattan-Guinness]].<ref name=":2" />

In 1965, Boyer was appointed associate editor of the ''[[Dictionary of Scientific Biography]]'', which was being planned by the [[American Council of Learned Societies]].<ref name=":0" /> He also contributed several articles to the ''[[Encyclopædia Britannica|Encyclopedia Britannica]]''<ref name=":3" /> and served as book-review editor of ''[[Scripta Mathematica]]'', published by [[Yeshiva University]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Scripta Mathematica|year = 1950|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zeQSAAAAIAAJ&q=%22Carl+B.+Boyer%22|access-date=2007-10-21}}</ref>

==Personal life and death==
He was married to Marjorie Boyer (née Nice), a professor of history. Boyer died of a [[myocardial infarction|heart attack]] at his home [[Brooklyn]], New York, on April 26, 1976. He was 69 years old.<ref name=":0" />

== Legacy ==
In 1978, Boyer's widow established the Carl B. Boyer Memorial Prize, to be awarded annually to an undergraduate at [[Columbia University]] who was not an American citizen for the best essay on a scientific or mathematical topic.<ref>{{cite web|title=Columbia College Bulletin:Prizes and Fellowships|url=http://www.college.columbia.edu/bulletin/prizes.php|access-date=2009-02-20|archive-date=2002-10-01|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021001225520/http://www.college.columbia.edu/bulletin/prizes.php|url-status=dead}}</ref>

According to [[Morris Kline]], Boyer played an instrumental role in establishing the history of mathematics as a worthwhile branch of study at a time when it was largely ignored in mainstream academic circles.<ref name=":3" />
